stem: A company provisions new servers by cloning a hardened, approved image. What is the BEST security benefit of this approach?

options.text: Consistent secure baselines are applied to every new system, reducing misconfiguration
options.rationale: Provisioning from a hardened baseline image ensures each system starts in a known-secure, consistent configuration, minimizing drift and misconfiguration.

options.text: Each server ends up uniquely and unpredictably configured
options.rationale: Unpredictable, inconsistent configuration is what baselines are meant to prevent.

options.text: Security patches become unnecessary
options.rationale: Baselines still require ongoing patching; they do not eliminate that need.

options.text: Servers no longer need access controls
options.rationale: A secure baseline includes, not replaces, access controls.

stem: When a new laptop is issued to an employee, what should be done FIRST to maintain accountability for the asset?

options.text: Record the asset in the inventory and assign ownership/custodianship
options.rationale: Recording the asset and assigning responsibility at issuance establishes accountability and enables tracking through its lifecycle.

options.text: Let the employee take it with no record
options.rationale: Issuing assets without records destroys accountability and tracking.

options.text: Disable all security features to speed setup
options.rationale: Disabling security during provisioning leaves the asset exposed.

options.text: Publicly post the device's serial number
options.rationale: Public disclosure of asset details is unnecessary and potentially risky.

stem: During provisioning, an administrator disables unused services, removes default apps, and closes unneeded ports. This MOST directly applies which principle?

options.text: Least functionality (reduce the attack surface)
options.rationale: Configuring a system to provide only necessary functions/services is the least-functionality principle, which shrinks the attack surface.

options.text: Maximum functionality for flexibility
options.rationale: Enabling everything increases attack surface, the opposite of the goal here.

options.text: Fail-open networking
options.rationale: Fail-open concerns failure behavior, not reducing enabled services.

options.text: Security through obscurity
options.rationale: Disabling real functionality is a concrete hardening measure, not mere obscurity.

stem: A new network appliance ships with a well-known default administrator password. During secure provisioning, what should be done FIRST?

options.text: Change the default credentials to a strong, unique password
options.rationale: Default credentials are publicly known and a top attack vector; changing them is a critical first hardening step.

options.text: Leave the default so support can access it easily
options.rationale: Leaving known default credentials is a severe, easily exploited weakness.

options.text: Publish the default password on the intranet
options.rationale: Publishing credentials broadens exposure and is grossly insecure.

options.text: Disable logging to reduce noise
options.rationale: Disabling logging harms detection and does not address the default-credential risk.

stem: A team repeatedly spins up cloud resources with inconsistent, sometimes insecure settings. What is the BEST way to provision securely and repeatably?

options.text: Use infrastructure-as-code with reviewed, hardened templates
options.rationale: IaC with vetted, hardened templates makes provisioning consistent, repeatable, reviewable, and secure by default.

options.text: Manually click through the console each time differently
options.rationale: Manual, inconsistent provisioning is exactly what causes the insecure drift described.

options.text: Grant every resource public internet access by default
options.rationale: Defaulting to public access dramatically increases exposure.

options.text: Skip all configuration review to move faster
options.rationale: Skipping review lets insecure configurations proliferate.

stem: A security configuration baseline is best defined as which of the following?

options.text: A documented, approved standard secure configuration for a type of system
options.rationale: A baseline is the approved minimum secure configuration standard from which systems are provisioned and against which drift is measured.

options.text: The maximum number of users a system can have
options.rationale: That describes a capacity limit, not a security baseline.

options.text: A list of the company's holidays
options.rationale: This is unrelated to configuration baselines.

options.text: The price paid for the hardware
options.rationale: Cost has nothing to do with a configuration baseline.

stem: When provisioning access for a new service account, which approach MOST reduces risk?

options.text: Grant only the specific permissions the service requires (least privilege)
options.rationale: Provisioning service accounts with only necessary permissions limits damage if the account is compromised.

options.text: Grant domain administrator rights for convenience
options.rationale: Over-privileged service accounts are a major risk if compromised.

options.text: Reuse a shared admin account for all services
options.rationale: Shared privileged accounts destroy accountability and expand exposure.

options.text: Give it access to everything just in case
options.rationale: Blanket access violates least privilege and increases blast radius.

stem: Refurbished drives from a retired project are being provisioned into new systems. What must occur FIRST?

options.text: Sanitize the drives to remove any residual data before reuse
options.rationale: Reused media may hold residual data (remanence); sanitizing first prevents old sensitive data from leaking into the new environment.

options.text: Deploy them immediately with old data intact
options.rationale: Deploying with residual data risks exposing prior sensitive information.

options.text: Assume the drives are already clean
options.rationale: Unverified assumptions about clean media invite remanence exposure.

options.text: Only relabel the drives
options.rationale: Relabeling does not remove residual data.

stem: An organization's hardened 'golden image' has not been updated in a year and now lacks recent patches. What is the BEST practice?

options.text: Regularly update and re-harden the baseline image so new systems inherit current patches
options.rationale: Baseline images must be kept current so every newly provisioned system starts patched and hardened, not with year-old vulnerabilities.

options.text: Keep using the stale image indefinitely
options.rationale: A stale image provisions systems with known, unpatched vulnerabilities.

options.text: Stop using images and configure each system randomly
options.rationale: Abandoning baselines reintroduces inconsistency and misconfiguration.

options.text: Delete the image and provision nothing
options.rationale: This blocks provisioning entirely rather than maintaining the baseline.

stem: To prevent unauthorized systems from appearing on the network, provisioning MOST importantly should include which control?

options.text: An authorization/approval step tied to inventory before a system goes live
options.rationale: Requiring approval and inventory registration before go-live prevents unauthorized 'shadow' systems from entering the environment untracked.

options.text: Allowing anyone to attach any device freely
options.rationale: Unrestricted device attachment is exactly what enables unauthorized systems.

options.text: Skipping inventory to save time
options.rationale: Skipping inventory removes the ability to detect unauthorized systems.

options.text: Disabling network monitoring
options.rationale: Disabling monitoring reduces the chance of detecting rogue systems.

stem: A team wants an authoritative reference for hardening operating systems during provisioning. Which is the BEST source?

options.text: Recognized hardening guides/benchmarks (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, vendor security guides)
options.rationale: Established benchmarks like CIS provide vetted, authoritative hardening configurations to base secure provisioning on.

options.text: A random blog post with no sourcing
options.rationale: Unvetted sources may give incomplete or incorrect hardening advice.

options.text: Whatever settings look nice
options.rationale: Aesthetic preference is not a basis for security hardening.

options.text: The default out-of-box configuration only
options.rationale: Defaults are typically not hardened and often include insecure settings.

stem: Systems provisioned securely gradually diverge from the baseline as ad hoc changes accumulate. This problem is MOST accurately called what?

options.text: Configuration drift
options.rationale: The gradual divergence of systems from their approved baseline over time is configuration drift, which must be detected and corrected.

options.text: Data remanence
options.rationale: Remanence is residual data on media, not configuration divergence.

options.text: Privilege escalation
options.rationale: Privilege escalation is gaining higher rights, not configuration divergence.

options.text: Load balancing
options.rationale: Load balancing distributes traffic and is unrelated to configuration divergence.

stem: To reduce risk from human error during setup, systems should be provisioned so that the default state is which of the following?

options.text: Secure by default (restrictive), with access opened only as needed
options.rationale: Secure-by-default provisioning starts restrictive and grants access deliberately, minimizing accidental exposure.

options.text: Fully open by default, locked down later if remembered
options.rationale: Open-by-default relies on someone remembering to secure it, which frequently fails.

options.text: Randomized so no one can predict it
options.rationale: Randomized configuration is inconsistent and unmanageable, not secure by design.

options.text: Identical to the vendor default with no changes
options.rationale: Vendor defaults are often insecure and should be hardened, not left as-is.

stem: What is the PRIMARY security advantage of automating resource provisioning with tested templates?

options.text: Consistent, repeatable, secure configurations that reduce human error
options.rationale: Automation applies the same vetted secure configuration every time, cutting the manual mistakes that cause insecure setups.

options.text: It removes the need to ever patch systems
options.rationale: Automation does not eliminate patching responsibilities.

options.text: It makes all data automatically public
options.rationale: Secure provisioning restricts access; it does not make data public.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any access control
options.rationale: Access controls remain essential and are part of secure provisioning.

stem: In asset security, 'secure provisioning' most directly refers to which of the following?

options.text: Deploying resources configured to meet security requirements from the start
options.rationale: Secure provisioning means setting up systems/resources with required security configurations built in from deployment.

options.text: Discarding all hardware upon purchase
options.rationale: That describes disposal, not provisioning.

options.text: Selling assets to third parties
options.rationale: Selling assets is unrelated to secure provisioning.

options.text: Ignoring configuration until an audit
options.rationale: Deferring configuration is the opposite of secure provisioning.

stem: A company issues hundreds of employee laptops. Which BEST ensures each is provisioned with required security controls?

options.text: Use centralized device management (MDM/endpoint management) to enforce a standard secure configuration
options.rationale: Centralized endpoint/MDM management enforces consistent security configuration, encryption, and policy across all issued devices at scale.

options.text: Let each user configure their own laptop however they like
options.rationale: User-configured devices produce inconsistent and often insecure setups.

options.text: Ship laptops with no security software
options.rationale: Shipping unprotected devices leaves endpoints vulnerable from day one.

options.text: Disable encryption to improve performance
options.rationale: Disabling encryption removes a key protection for data at rest.

stem: An administrator wants to update the approved hardened baseline for all future systems. What is the BEST process to follow?

options.text: Route the baseline change through change management for review and approval before adoption
options.rationale: Baseline changes affect all future systems and should go through change control so they are reviewed, tested, and approved before adoption.

options.text: Silently change the baseline with no review
options.rationale: Unreviewed baseline changes can introduce weaknesses across every new system.

options.text: Let each admin keep a personal baseline
options.rationale: Personal baselines reintroduce inconsistency and undermine standardization.

options.text: Never update the baseline
options.rationale: Baselines must evolve with new patches/threats; freezing them causes stale insecurity.

stem: For laptops that will store sensitive data, which control is MOST important to enable during provisioning?

options.text: Full-disk encryption
options.rationale: Enabling FDE at provisioning ensures data at rest is protected before any sensitive data is stored on the device.

options.text: A screensaver slideshow
options.rationale: A screensaver does not protect stored data.

options.text: Extra desktop shortcuts
options.rationale: Shortcuts have no security relevance.

options.text: A brighter keyboard backlight
options.rationale: Backlighting is irrelevant to data protection.

stem: After provisioning a system from a baseline, what should be done FIRST to confirm it meets requirements before go-live?

options.text: Validate the configuration against the baseline (e.g., a compliance scan/checklist)
options.rationale: Verifying the provisioned system against the baseline confirms controls are correctly applied before it goes into production.

options.text: Immediately expose it to the internet untested
options.rationale: Exposing an unverified system risks deploying misconfigurations to production.

options.text: Delete the baseline documentation
options.rationale: Deleting documentation removes the reference needed for verification.

options.text: Grant all users admin rights
options.rationale: Blanket admin rights violate least privilege and are not a verification step.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant to securely provisioning a new server?

options.text: The color of the server rack door
options.rationale: Rack door color has no bearing on secure provisioning of the server, making it least relevant.

options.text: Applying a hardened baseline configuration
options.rationale: Hardened baselines are central to secure provisioning.

options.text: Changing default credentials
options.rationale: Changing defaults is a critical provisioning hardening step.

options.text: Registering the server in the asset inventory
options.rationale: Inventory registration is important for accountability and tracking.
